title: Colliding Worlds
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reflects on how recognizing women practitioners within their Soto Zen community has rejuvenated them, reminding them of the importance of connection and being part of a broader movement. This experience has also made them realize that their own group may be more focused on individual practice than community activities, prompting them to consider whether they should continue as a sitting group or expand into a Zen center with more events.

sentences.text: Well, originally tonight we're going to have a visiting speaker, visiting priest, our friend and colleague Rick Spencer.
Rick has been car-free for decades, and so he was going to take the bus down here from Vancouver, but he missed the bus, so he sends his apologies.
There's only like a bus at two and then not until seven, so it didn't work.
But he'll also come next week.
We worked it out and I assured him that we would be delighted to have him next week.
So we'll have a lot of talks.
I'll give a talk now, and next Wednesday night Rick will give a talk.
And then actually the Wednesday after that, Terry Thompson will give a talk reflecting on his experiences on the mountains and rivers, a hiking retreat.
Since I only found out at 2:15 that I was going to give a talk, I don't have a whole lot prepared.
As we were doing this great little ritual, the thought popped into my mind, which it would, that I don't have a very good talk, and my talk is probably not deserving of this lofty ritual.
Then I realized, well, wait a minute, maybe all talks are worthy of love and attention and ritual, like the simple act of opening your mouth to say anything.
Wouldn't it be good if before we ever said anything to anybody, we offered incense, made prostrations, settled ourselves in our seat, and thought carefully about what we're going to say?
This would be good, huh?
So now I feel better again.
Thank you very much for listening to my talk.
I have actually sort of three different topics.
The first is, I thought I'd give you a little trip report.
I spent last weekend in Oregon, I think it was last weekend, at the national meeting of the Soto Zen Buddhist Association, which is an organization of American Soto Zen priests, actually.
To be a member of the organization, you have to be a priest.
So it's pretty fun, hanging out with fifty or sixty, mostly American priests, a few from other places.
But then there's two kinds of membership.
The first kind is the associate member, which is what I am, I'm an associate member.
These are the priests still in training under their teacher.
And then there're the full members who are the priests who've received Dharma transmission.
We have this system of color coding, so you can tell them apart.

The black is the associate members, and then the full members are in brown, with this robe, when we're in the formal practice time, wearing a lot of robes, and then the smaller robe like John has, and Nancy has on, they're all color coded.
The full members had a lot of work to do.
They had all these business meetings because they're basically trying to sort of chart the course of the American Zen movement.
As you would expect, all of them are pretty busy running centers, or running around giving retreats, or writing books, or that kind of thing.
So they don't have a whole lot of time for this.
Because of that, they don't meet that often.
The whole group only meets every two years.
They also have committees and a board and all that stuff, and phone meetings, and email lists, and all that we know about.
Anyway, they were trying to decide things like, what should the requirements be in American Zen for being a priest?
Big topics.
Or another thing they were trying to decide was, should we in our formal Zen practice recognize women practitioners?
As many of you know, in our formal practice, we don't do that often here, but you often will recite or invoke in some way a list of names of ancestors.
The Buddha, and the Buddha's student, Mahakasyapa, Mahakasyapa's student, Ananda.
This makes this chain, ninety-three, ninety-four actually to me.
It means ninety-three or ninety-four, I forget, names from Buddha to me.
Which is kind of wild if you think about it, right?
Two thousand, five hundred years.
It's only like one hundred people.
You could fit them all in this room if they were standing.
It would be a code violation, but you could fit them.
Anyway, they've been trying to decide for a while, that's a beautiful religious notion, this lineage.

The thought that, and they have beautiful language to describe this, the thought that there's some understanding, some lived understanding that comes to you only through years of meditation practice of what this life is at its deepest level.

That that's something that by sort of practicing with somebody and rubbing shoulders and being in conversation with them over many years and conversations, verbal and nonverbal conversations, there's something that can be transmitted on.
So they use phrases like warm hand to warm hand, or warm heart to warm heart, these body analogies, shoulder to shoulder, some of which we use in English.

The Soto Zen Buddhist Association full members were trying to decide in addition to chanting and having special documents made that show this list of ninety-four men, because of course they are all men, because that's who writes history.
Maybe we should include women.
Since we don't have sort of long, the list of men is deeply historically based.
It's not exactly literally true.
A fair amount of it was invented in the eleventh and twelfth centuries in China, but it's old, you know what I mean?
And we all agree on it because it's what the tradition has passed forward.

We don't have that kind of religious tradition or historical documentation or even sort of pseudo-historical religion, their documentation to decide which women exactly, do you include this one or that one?
And do they have to be related in a certain way?
Are you really trying to find a woman who was a student of another woman?
What about a woman who was a student of a man, or a man who was a student of a woman?
So it gets, as you can imagine, the meetings get contentious fast.
What about so and so?
They were working on that, and I'm happy to report that they did decide yes, which took them about a decade to decide.
Yes, we will have a list of women, ancestors, and once the dust settles on the exact names, I was given a handout, which I'm told not to share yet with the names because it's going to get tweaked.
So then when we do formal ceremonies and ordinations where you receive the male lineage, you also would receive the woman's lineage, and we'll do it retroactively, too.
People who have already received this thing will receive this document.
Anyway, they're working hard doing that.

We just got to sit in on the final meeting, and even that there was a fair amount of, it just looked like any other consensus meeting, lots of off-topic, and it turns out that thirty or forty years of meditation practice does not make you any good at meetings.
Maybe it works.

The us, the black guys, we just say we're probably there just because with us they're watching, they would probably be embarrassed to be too, you know, what I mean, to be too self-centered and, you know, divisive and stuff like that.
So they did decide on that, and they're trying to decide on lots of other things.
Meanwhile, the associate members just pretty much got to hang around and have conversations, but didn't have any hard work to do, and go to dinner and meet people and stuff like that.
I'll tell you a little bit about the place where it was, and it was really helpful to me actually.
It was lovely to be reminded of what we know intellectually, that what we're doing here at Red Cedar Zen Community is part of something bigger.
It's not just something we invented in nineteen ninety-one in Bellingham, Washington, and kind of kept up.
You can know that in one way right in your head, but you actually have to really go somewhere and be with people and have conversations.
I remembered to really feel that sense of connection and of being part of a broader movement, just full of wonderful people, really wonderful wise people.
And I got to see people I hadn't seen for fifteen or twenty years from when I practiced at the monasteries in San Francisco.
As coarse as you would be, I was a little shy about introducing myself.
But they all remembered me.
It's nice, you know.
Plus Norman was running around talking about us, it turns out too.
So they knew all about Bellingham.
Norman told me.
Anyway, a little bit about the meeting and a little about the place, because I think it would be a good thing if we felt some connection to this place.

Nine years ago, not that long ago, the Zen Community of Oregon, which is a group not, you know, a little bigger than this one, but not hugely bigger, not like orders of magnitude bigger, it's a little bigger.
Zen Community of Oregon, which has two teachers, Chosen and Hogan Bays, they're a married couple.

So a place big enough for quite a few people to live full time, do lots of meditation practice, lots of zazen, and live a very immersive life of practice.

So, for a long time they had a vision of having a training monastery, but they were starting just where we're starting, you know.

And somehow, nine years ago, after exhaustive searchings and falls starts, they found an elementary school outside of the little town called Clatskanie, which is just right off of the Columbia River, the lower Columbia.

In Oregon, they gutted the property tax rolls.
And so the schools are now operating on like forty percent or fifty percent or something like that, what they had at the peak.
So the schools are broke, like literally.
They've cut all these, it's terrible actually.
They've cut all these programs.
And the school districts are all broke.
It turns out this particular district had a school they didn't need anymore.
And so they sold, so they got a fire sale school.
The Zen Community of Oregon bought the school for a million, I mean, not for nothing, for a million dollars.
Put our rent in perspective there for a million dollars.
But they've, they really wanted to make it work out the best for the school board.
So the school board financed it for them.

So now they have this full size elementary school.
Suddenly just have, not just gradually build buildings, but suddenly have all these buildings.
They've created, as they plan, they've created this training monastery.
There are about twenty residents there full time, as well as the two teachers.
Then they have a sesshin, five to seven day intensive retreat every month and have done since they walked in the door.
So, twelve times a year for nine years, and they just keep going.
Shorter retreats in between the daily schedule includes a wake up bell at three fifty in the morning and then meditation all morning until a long morning service and formal meals.
I don't know if they have meals in the meditation all the time or not.

I don't know the exact schedule, but the point being a very strong emphasis on continuous sustained zazen practice, very quiet, most that we were there yacking away, but usually it's very quiet place.
Very little talking, lots of practice and something about the rigor and the place and the excitement of being something with something new.
They've attracted quite a few younger members too, which is something Americans and sanghas worry about.
We worry a little bit about everyone's gonna be over sixty and then they're gonna be over seventy and they're gonna be over eighty and then that's it.
So they've attracted several youngest people and they have a sort of formal priest training program, a little much more formal and organized than Norman does with me and my colleagues.
One of the commitments involved in ordaining as a priest in their system is that you would live in the monastery full time for five years.
So they have eight or nine priests in training and another dozen or so living there, taking care of the place, cooking the meals, cleaning the hallways, sitting zazen.
The other thing they have is, but it's not all like dour, hardcore zazen, the other thing they have is a marimba band.

So the last night of our meeting, they tried it out the marimba band and it was fantastic, like a really good marimba band too, like they don't do anything half cocked here, you know, it's like serious zazen, serious marimba, you know.
It turns out one of the two teachers had some kind of background in that and found a teacher to work with them.
The other thing they do with their marimba band is they go into the schools.
So these young Zen monks with their shaved heads and their Samoai and they're and they go by their Japanese darmananes too.
It's a full on thing.

Go into the elementary schools with their marimbas, you know, and so Kojen and Dai Tetsu and Ryushin go and teach the kids music because the schools don't have music programs anymore because of the funding.
I guess every single public school arts teacher in Oregon has been laid off.
So watch out for whoever the Tim Lyman is down there was more successful, you know, than ours.
Thank goodness our guy's not that good.
Anyway, I just want to tell you a little bit about the trip.

One thing that I found really interesting and helpful and I want to mention what I'm thinking about and probably this is a longer conversation, but to plant some seeds and we can talk about this more later.
Some of us are sort of been around a while and some not so much.
So this is a little bit my sort of musing about where we are as a sangha and some possibilities.
What became clear to me in conversation with sort of larger, more established centers and also centers where the priests are supported and get to work full time, you don't have an outside job.
What I realized is that there's sort of like two, roughly two categories of Zen community in America, with some overlap.
One is the sitting group, which is a wonderful thing.
A sitting group is for the most part a small group of friends.
Everyone knows each other usually would have one or maybe two sort of primary weekly meetings.
It keeps things pretty simple, maybe a few retreats.
But the main point of a sitting group being a community of friends supporting each other and just coming to sit, coming to sit.
Most of the things that a sitting group would do would be for support of that group of people, to make it possible to get a place where it's comfortable to do the sitting, to help each other.
Not forget to come to provide a little bit of teaching and resources and so on to just make it all sort of make sense and fit into their lives.
So that group of people who know each other and somehow has come to practice can keep going, because we know if we were just on our own, there's not too many of us, I think that would keep this up.
One gets a little distracted.
So that's one possibility.
The other possibility is a Zen center, and a Zen center seems to have all that in its way, but a Zen center seems to have more of an outward facing focus.

And so a Zen center would, in every case that I know of, have a large Saturday or Sunday public program with a public talk, with Zazen instruction offered in a very clear way, with lots of people coming every time, and there are new people.

Not everybody probably knows everybody; maybe they wear name tags, and there's probably a core of people who do know each other pretty well, and they were probably from the sitting groups that evolved into this.
And a Zen center was likely also more likely to have a family program and be meeting the needs of families a little bit better.
And one of those that I heard quite a bit about is in Portland, Oregon, Dharma Reign Zen community.
They have something called Dharma school, which I think is the largest Zen center family program in the world, probably.
And they told me that they had to buy a whole other building to handle Dharma school, and they get one hundred to one hundred fifty kids every other Sunday for Dharma school.
And they have six rate classes by age group.

And that he told me, we don't really worry about attracting young people because we have lots of young people, partly because the people who are twenty, twenty-one are really excited to hang out with the eight-year-old kids and teach at Dharma school.

So like the twenty-somethings hang out with the kids, and then the parents are liberated from being with the kids and they get to go into the grown-up groups, and everybody's happy on three generations.
And so I just had never really thought about that way.
I think I had, there's a way that you can kind of feel like we should be doing more, we should be doing this, we should be doing that.
And if you're a sitting group, why would you, you know what I mean?
It's like a pain in the butt, it's complicated, it's expensive, you know.
You kind of lose some intimacy, and you don't know anybody anymore, and it's really busy and you have lots of meetings to get it organized.
So if you're a sitting group, maybe you just should happily be a sitting group.
There's nothing wrong with that.
But if you're, and if you're a Zen center, you know, maybe then you're concerned about, oh, we lost our sense of intimacy.
How do we stay connected?
Do we need affinity groups?
Do we need small groups?
Do we need to sort of stay that keeps a sense of intimacy and connection.
And so what it made me realize is we are essentially like a sitting group.
We are a sitting group.
We don't have all this sort of public outward looking stuff.
Once in a while we do something, right?
We had that Buddhism and Bellingham series, but the Zen centers do that year round.
It's a one-time thing.
We're essentially a sitting group.
You know, we're in a building that could be a Zen center, probably just big enough.
And so we kind of, in a way we have a sort of choice point.
And so I just, what I'm thinking about, should we be happily a sitting group and enjoy each other and practice and settle our hearts and enjoy our lives?
That's wonderful.
Or should we open things up and be more of a Zen center, or maybe it's possible to be some of both in certain ways.
So anyway, this seems sort of obvious now I say it, but I had to talk to these other teachers over dinner, and they said, oh yeah, what do you do?
What's your public program like on the weekend?
Oh, ours is so popular, man.
It's like gangbusters.
Oh, like, what classes do you teach?
Once in a while we have a quarterly thing.
So if you're a Zen group, that's like pretty subpar.
I mean, if you're a Zen center, but if you're a sitting group, like, oh, that's great.
John's doing the thing this Saturday, four-hour class.
That's nice.
Sitting group doing that.
That's good.
So I don't know.
That was useful to sort of get the sense of choose as a community what you want to do, and then you don't have to feel like you're missing out on anything.
And they're also various anyway, not to make this into a big business meeting, but that was one of the things I learned at the meeting.
There are various economies of scale.
You get to a certain size and then you can start supporting people and then other things suddenly become much more possible.
Right.
I mean, if I was full time for the Zen center, some of the things that are like, oh God, impossible, we can do it.
It would just be like, no big deal.
I'm here anyway, I'll take care of it.
Or if we had a halftime administrator who was paid, then adding one more event and having registration for one more event would be like, no problem.

It's amazing that what we do, what we do, there may be in a way where a sitting group that temporarily becomes a Zen center periodically when Norman Fischer shows up in town and kind of like, oh my God, there's eighty people in the room.
So anyway, some of the things I learned at the Soto Zen Buddhist Association meeting, that was the first chapter of the talk.

Before I was down at the veterans hospital in Seattle as a volunteer and observing classes and in conversations and just kind of trying to help out a little bit.

Like what's that?
After I'll read it, you know?
So I, and it takes, and then there's like a month or more of scheduling in between each meeting because of how backed up they are and all this.

I was like, wow, about buddies who were gone.
Yeah.
And so anyway, I was in there.

I never can be.
Reasons, which I still think are probably good reasons.

about the circle of the way, the circle of the way, or the great way.
